title: Dickinson v. Dodds
lead: A prospective buyer tried to accept before the seller’s promised Friday deadline, but first learned that the property had been sold to someone else; without a paid-for option, the deadline did not preserve an already withdrawn offer.

actors.name: John Dodds
actors.role: Property owner who made the initial proposal

actors.name: Berry
actors.role: Source of information about the sale and later Dickinson’s acceptance messenger

actors.name: Mrs. Burgess
actors.role: Dodds’s mother-in-law who received an attempted acceptance

actors.name: Vice-Chancellor Bacon, James L.J., and Mellish L.J.
actors.role: Trial judge and authors of the appellate judgments

proceedings: Vice-Chancellor Bacon ordered specific performance; Dodds and Allan appealed; Court of Appeal reversed and dismissed Dickinson’s bill with costs, including both defendants’ appeal costs.
limits: The operative reasoning depends on Dickinson’s actual knowledge before acceptance, not a secret sale automatically revoking an offer. Bacon’s reasoning was reversed trial analysis, not an appellate dissent. Priority between two binding purchase contracts was reserved.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Dodds offered the property and promised time to decide
sections.cue: Distinguish the sale proposal from a purchased option.
paragraphs: On Wednesday, June 10, 1874, John Dodds signed and delivered a memorandum proposing to sell George Dickinson dwelling houses, garden ground, stabling, and related outbuildings at Croft for £800. Although it began with agreement-like wording, a signed postscript called it an offer to remain open until Friday, June 12, at nine in the morning.

Dickinson wanted time to decide and gave nothing in exchange for the promise to keep it open. Both apparently believed the deadline prevented withdrawal, but their shared assumption later proved mistaken. Dickinson’s bill alleged that he decided to accept Thursday morning but did not communicate because he believed he could wait until Friday.

sections.title: News of Allan’s purchase preceded Dickinson’s delivery attempts
sections.cue: Preserve the knowledge finding and the actual purchase price.
paragraphs: Thursday afternoon, Berry told Dickinson that Dodds had been offering or agreeing to sell to Thomas Allan. The report uses varying descriptions of the information, but the appellate judgments treated Dickinson’s allegations and conduct as establishing that he knew, before attempting acceptance, that Dodds had changed position and actually agreed to sell to Allan. The reasoning did not rest on an unexplained rumor.

At about 7:30 Thursday evening, Dickinson left formal written acceptance with Mrs. Burgess, Dodds’s mother-in-law, at whose house Dodds was staying. She testified that she forgot to deliver it. Around seven Friday morning, Berry, now acting for Dickinson, handed Dodds a duplicate at Darlington railway station. Dodds replied that Dickinson was too late because the property was sold. Dickinson soon tendered another duplicate as Dodds entered a railway carriage; Dodds again refused. All preceded nine o’clock, but followed the knowledge the appellate court treated as withdrawal.

Dodds had signed a formal sale agreement with Allan on Thursday, June 11, for the same £800 and received a £40 deposit. Whether Allan knew of Dickinson’s earlier offer was disputed. There was no finding of a higher price; a later judicial hypothetical about a more favorable offer did not describe this transaction. Berry was not identified as Dodds’s authorized revocation agent.

sections.title: The trial judge treated timely acceptance as relating back
sections.cue: Explain why the decree affected both defendants.
paragraphs: Dickinson sought specific performance against Dodds, an injunction preventing conveyance to Allan, and, if conveyance occurred, an order treating Allan as trustee and requiring him to convey to Dickinson. He also requested damages. Each demand depended on an enforceable right preceding Allan’s.

In January 1876, Vice-Chancellor Bacon read the memorandum and postscript together as a sufficiently definite engagement. He considered acceptance within the stated period effective and related it back to the original date, so Dodds’s intervening agreement could not defeat Dickinson’s equitable interest. Bacon ordered specific performance, declared Allan had no interest, and allowed Dickinson to deduct suit costs from the price. Both Dodds and Allan appealed.

sections.title: James treated the original writing as a revocable offer
sections.cue: Identify why knowledge mattered more than the final hour.
paragraphs: Lord Justice James rejected the premise that the memorandum already bound both parties to a sale. Dickinson’s wish to decide later and the postscript’s description showed an unaccepted offer. The additional promise of time lacked consideration. The £800 would support a sale if acceptance occurred while the offer remained open; it did not separately purchase the opportunity to accept until Friday.

No particular formula of personal, express revocation was required on these facts. Dickinson already knew Dodds had agreed to sell elsewhere and no longer intended the proposed bargain with him. James read the hurried acceptances as efforts to hold Dodds to the mistaken view that the Friday deadline made withdrawal impossible. Once Dickinson had information equivalent to withdrawal, the messenger’s lack of authority to revoke did not preserve the offer.

Without an enforceable option, the deadline marked the outside time for accepting a continuing offer; it did not protect the offer against earlier withdrawal. The decisive sequence was knowledge before attempted acceptance, not an attempted acceptance before nine o’clock. Mrs. Burgess’s failure to deliver was part of the story, but the court did not announce a categorical rule about acceptances left with relatives.

sections.title: Mellish agreed and separated the writing requirement from actual agreement
sections.cue: Keep his reserved priority question distinct from the result.
paragraphs: Lord Justice Mellish likewise treated the proposal as revocable and Dickinson’s knowledge of the completed agreement with Allan as fatal to later acceptance. His horse-sale and death-of-offeror analogies illustrated that conclusion; his application repeatedly depended on knowledge, rather than a rule that unknown intervening conduct automatically extinguished an offer.

Mellish explained that a signed land offer could in principle become binding against its signer through verbal acceptance satisfying the Statute of Frauds. A sufficient written memorandum and formation of an actual agreement were separate questions. The writing did not prove acceptance before the offer ceased to be available.

He assumed for argument that Allan knew of the earlier proposal but found no bar to Allan contracting while Dickinson held only a revocable offer. Because Dickinson never formed a binding sale contract, the court did not need to decide priority between two binding purchasers. Mellish expressly reserved that hypothetical question despite also observing that Allan’s agreement came first.

sections.title: Dickinson lost specific performance and bore both appeal costs
sections.cue: Conclude with the complementary appellate judgments.
paragraphs: James and Mellish reached the same result, and Baggallay concurred in both judgments without separate analysis. The Court of Appeal reversed Bacon’s decree and dismissed Dickinson’s bill with costs. After argument over whether costs should attach to one or both appeals, Dickinson was required to pay the costs of both Dodds’s and Allan’s appeals. He received no damages.

The judgment removed the premise for relief against either defendant: Dickinson had no sale contract. The reporter’s tentative broader suggestion that a sale alone could revoke without notice did not supply the operative holding. The appellate result rested on an unsupported promise to hold open and Dickinson’s actual knowledge before acceptance.
